{{short description|Special forms of a typed lambda calculus}}
In [[mathematical logic]], '''System U''' and '''System U<sup>−</sup>''' are [[pure type system]]s, i.e. special forms of a [[typed lambda calculus]] with an arbitrary number of [[Structure (mathematical logic)#Many-sorted structures|sorts]], axioms and rules (or dependencies between the sorts). 

System U was proved inconsistent by [[Jean-Yves Girard]] in 1972<ref name="Girard1972">{{cite web |first=Jean-Yves |last=Girard |title=Interprétation fonctionnelle et Élimination des coupures de l'arithmétique d'ordre supérieur |year=1972 |url=https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~kw/scans/girard72thesis.pdf }}</ref> (and the question of consistency of System U<sup>−</sup> was formulated). This result led to the realization that [[Per Martin-Löf|Martin-Löf]]'s original [[intuitionistic type theory#Martin-Löf type theories|1971 type theory]] was inconsistent, as it allowed the same "type in type" behaviour that Girard's paradox exploits.

== Formal definition ==
System U is defined<ref name=SoerensenUrzyczyn2006>{{cite book |first1=Morten Heine |last1=Sørensen |first2=Paweł |last2=Urzyczyn |title=Lectures on the Curry–Howard isomorphism |publisher=Elsevier |year=2006 |isbn=0-444-52077-5 |chapter=Pure type systems and the lambda cube|doi=10.1016/S0049-237X(06)80015-7 }}</ref>{{rp|352}} as a pure type system with
* three [[Many-sorted logic|sorts]] <math>\{\ast, \square, \triangle\}</math>;
* two axioms <math>\{\ast:\square, \square:\triangle\}</math>; and
* five rules <math>\{(\ast,\ast), (\square,\ast), (\square,\square), (\triangle,\ast), (\triangle,\square)\}</math>.

System U<sup>−</sup> is defined the same with the exception of the <math>(\triangle, \ast)</math> rule.

The sorts <math>\ast</math> and <math>\square</math> are conventionally called “type” and “[[kind (type theory)|kind]]”, respectively; the sort <math>\triangle</math> doesn't have a specific name. The two axioms describe the containment of types in kinds (<math>\ast:\square</math>) and kinds in <math>\triangle</math> (<math>\square:\triangle</math>). Intuitively, the sorts describe a hierarchy in the ''nature'' of the terms.
#   All values have a ''type'', such as a base type (''e.g.'' <math>b : \mathrm{Bool}</math> is read as “<math>b</math> is a boolean”) or a (dependent) function type (''e.g.'' <math>f : \mathrm{Nat} \to \mathrm{Bool}</math> is read as “<math>f</math> is a function from natural numbers to booleans”).
#   <math>\ast</math> is the sort of all such types (<math>t : \ast</math> is read as “<math>t</math> is a type”). From <math>\ast</math> we can build more terms, such as <math>\ast \to \ast</math> which is the ''kind'' of unary type-level operators (''e.g.'' <math>\mathrm{List} : \ast \to \ast</math> is read as “<math>\mathrm{List}</math> is a function from types to types”, that is, a polymorphic type). The rules restrict how we can form new kinds.
#   <math>\square</math> is the sort of all such kinds (<math>k : \square</math> is read as “<math>k</math> is a kind”). Similarly we can build related terms, according to what the rules allow.
#   <math>\triangle</math> is the sort of all such terms.

The rules govern the dependencies between the sorts: <math>(\ast,\ast)</math> says that values may depend on values ([[first-class function|functions]]), <math>(\square,\ast)</math> allows values to depend on types ([[parametric polymorphism|polymorphism]]), <math>(\square,\square)</math> allows types to depend on types ([[type constructor|type operators]]), and so on.

== Girard's paradox<!--'Girard's paradox' redirects here--> ==
The definitions of System U and U<sup>−</sup> allow the assignment of [[parametric polymorphism|polymorphic]] [[kind (type theory)|kind]]s to ''generic constructors'' in analogy to polymorphic types of terms in classical polymorphic lambda calculi, such as [[System F]]. An example of such a generic constructor might be{{r|SoerensenUrzyczyn2006|page=353}} (where ''k'' denotes a kind variable)

:<math>\lambda k^\square \lambda\alpha^{k \to k} \lambda\beta^k\!. \alpha (\alpha \beta) \;:\; \Pi k : \square.((k \to k) \to k \to k)</math>.

This mechanism is sufficient to construct a term with the type <math>(\forall p:\ast, p)</math> (equivalent to the type <math> \bot</math>), which implies that every type is [[type inhabitation|inhabited]]. By the [[Curry–Howard correspondence]], this is equivalent to all logical propositions being provable, which makes the system inconsistent.

Girard's paradox is the [[type theory|type-theoretic]] analogue of the [[Burali-Forti paradox]] in [[naive set theory|set theory]].<ref name="Coquand1986">{{cite book |first=Thierry |last=Coquand |author-link=Thierry Coquand |chapter=An analysis of Girard's paradox |title=Logic in Computer Science |pages=227–236 |publisher=[[IEEE Computer Society]] Press |year=1986 }}</ref>
